title: JESUS KNEW PETER WOULD DENY HIM—AND STILL WASHED HIS FEET
paragraphs: JESUS KNEW PETER WOULD DENY HIM—AND STILL WASHED HIS FEET
He already knew the sound of Peter’s denial before Peter ever heard the rooster crow. He knew the fear, the failure, the shame, and the bitter tears that were coming. And still… Jesus knelt.
There is something important we need to correct before we go any further.
Peter did not betray Jesus in the same specific sense that Judas betrayed Him. Judas deliberately handed Jesus over to His enemies. Peter denied knowing Him.
But perhaps what makes Peter’s story so devastating is that his failure feels painfully familiar.
Peter believed he would remain faithful.
Maybe that is why this story gets so close to the heart.
Because some of our worst failures did not happen because we stopped believing in Jesus.
They happened while we still loved Him.
We just discovered that our courage was weaker than we thought.
Our flesh was weaker than we admitted.
Our fear was stronger than our promises.
Before Peter failed publicly, Jesus knew privately.
The meal is underway. The shadow of the cross is already stretching across the evening. Jesus knows where He is going. He knows what Judas is preparing to do. He knows His disciples will scatter.

εἰς τέλος ἠγάπησεν αὐτούς
eis telos ēgapēsen autous
The expression εἰς τέλος — eis telos carries the sense of love reaching its end, its completion, its full extent.
Jesus was not running out of love as His disciples were running out of courage.
Then something happens that should make every proud heart uncomfortable.
He lays aside His outer garments.
He pours water into a basin.
And the hands that would soon be pierced begin washing dirty feet.
“After that he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples’ feet…”
Maybe he sees another disciple’s feet enter the basin.

“What I do thou knowest not now; but thou shalt know hereafter.”
—John 13:7
The Greek is even more forceful:
Οὐ μὴ νίψῃς μου τοὺς πόδας εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα.
Ou mē nipsēs mou tous podas eis ton aiōna.
In effect: You will certainly never wash my feet.
Peter still thinks discipleship is partly about proving how devoted he is to Jesus.
Jesus is about to teach him that salvation begins somewhere far more humbling:
letting Jesus do for you what you cannot do for yourself.
“Jesus answered him, If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me.”
Peter immediately swings to the other extreme.
“Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head.”
But here is what should stop us.
Jesus is washing the feet of a man whose future failure He already knows.
Those feet will soon carry Peter into a courtyard where fear will expose him.
Peter still believes his loyalty is stronger than it really is.

“Though all men shall be offended because of thee, yet will I never be offended.”
—Matthew 26:33
Peter essentially looks at the possibility of everyone else falling and says:
The dangerous confidence of a believer who has not yet discovered how desperately he needs grace.

“Verily I say unto thee, That this night, before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice.”
—Matthew 26:34
“Though I should die with thee, yet will I not deny thee.”
That is what makes this hurt.
Peter was not necessarily lying when he promised loyalty.
He simply did not know Peter as well as Jesus knew Peter.
And maybe you know what that feels like.
Then one day you looked in the mirror and hardly recognized yourself.
The browser history nobody knows about.
The conversation where you were embarrassed to admit you follow Christ.
The money you knew was becoming your master.
The applause you wanted more than obedience.
The prayer life that slowly disappeared.
The private sin living behind a public Christian image.
The resentment dressed up as discernment.
The version of yourself everybody sees…
and the version God sees when nobody else is looking.
And Peter denies Jesus a third time.
Luke records one of the most haunting details in the entire Passion narrative:

“And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter.”
—Luke 22:61
Peter has barely finished denying Him.
The Greek verb Luke uses is ἐνέβλεψεν — eneblepsen, from emblepō, describing a direct, intent look.

“And Peter went out, and wept bitterly.”
—Luke 22:62
Others come from finally seeing yourself clearly.
Peter had just discovered something terrifying:
He was capable of doing the very thing he was certain he would never do.
Maybe you have had your rooster-crow moment.
That moment when the excuses stopped working.
When nobody found out—but the Holy Spirit would not let you pretend anymore.
“I denied Him with my life even when my lips still called Him Lord.”
And this is where shame begins whispering its favorite theology.
Real Christians don't fail like this.
when He picked up the towel.
Jesus knew about the courtyard when He picked up the towel.
This does not make Peter’s sin insignificant.
Grace never requires us to rename sin.
Biblical grace is not Jesus saying sin does not matter.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God went to Calvary.
But grace declares something equally astonishing:
your sin does not have to write the final chapter when Christ becomes the Author of your redemption.
Jesus had already told Peter something remarkable before Peter fell.

“Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat: But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren.”
—Luke 22:31–32
Jesus does not say, “If you return.”
He says, “when thou art converted”—in context, when you turn back.
καὶ σύ ποτε ἐπιστρέψας στήρισον τοὺς ἀδελφούς σου
kai sy pote epistrepsas stērison tous adelphous sou
“When you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.”
Before Peter falls, Jesus speaks beyond Peter’s fall.
Before Peter breaks, Jesus sees restoration.
Before Peter denies Him, Jesus sees a restored disciple strengthening others.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Redeeming the person inside the scandal.
And this is where Peter’s story becomes our story.
The Gospel is not the announcement that good people managed to become good enough for God.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners who could never rescue themselves were pursued by a Savior who could.
He went willingly to the cross.
Forgiveness is not God lowering His standard until our sin becomes acceptable.
Forgiveness was purchased at terrible cost.
Peter could not wash away Peter’s denial.
You cannot wash away yours either.
But Jesus can make sinners clean.
That basin in the upper room points our eyes toward something infinitely greater than water.
Toward the Savior who does not merely improve guilty people but reconciles sinners to God.
And after the resurrection, Jesus goes looking for Peter.
John 21 brings us to another fire.
Peter denied Jesus near a charcoal fire.
John 18:18 uses the Greek word ἀνθρακιά — anthrakia, a charcoal fire.
Then, after the resurrection, John 21:9 uses that same unusual word.
You can almost smell Peter’s memory burning.
Jesus does not restore Peter by pretending nothing happened.
“Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?”
And each time, Jesus redirects Peter outward.
Peter’s failure would not become his final identity.
The mouth that denied Jesus would proclaim Him.
The frightened disciple would become a witness.
The broken man would strengthen his brothers.
Grace did not merely comfort Peter.
That is why this message cannot end with, “Don't worry about your sin because Jesus understands.”
Grace does not make peace with the darkness destroying you.
Grace brings you out of it.
Maybe the question is not whether Jesus knows your worst moment.
The question is what you will do now that you know He already knows.
Or will you come into the light?
Will you keep defending the thing Christ is calling you to surrender?
There is no secret confession you need to type publicly to earn forgiveness.

“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.”
—Ephesians 2:8
But if this story exposed something you have been hiding, do not waste that conviction.
Then think of one Peter in your life.
Someone ashamed of what they have done.
Someone who believes failure has disqualified them forever.
Someone who thinks Jesus could never want them after what happened.
But the deepest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelievers to follow too.
But before you leave, remember the scene.
Peter does not yet hear the rooster.
Peter does not yet feel the terror of that courtyard.
Peter does not yet taste the bitterness of those tears.
Peter does not yet know how badly Peter is going to fail.
And Jesus is already on His knees.
Love moving toward a man who will soon swear that he does not know Him.
That is the terrifying beauty of a Savior who knows the truth about us before we finally admit it ourselves—and still calls us to repent, come home, be cleansed, and follow Him.
The rooster may expose your failure.
But it does not get to write your ending.
